content.content: # Job — Extend the task tracker The directory holds a working program in Rust: a task tracker that reads commands from a file and reports what it did. Extend it. The program's source is at `src/main.rs`. Build and run it with `cargo` and `clippy`. ## What it already does The first command-line argument is the path of a text file holding one command per line. Blank lines are ignored. | Command | What it does | |---|---| | `add ` | Records a task, open, and writes `added <id>`. Ids start at 1 and count up. The title is the rest of the line and may hold spaces. | | `done <id>` | Marks that task finished and writes `done <id>`; writes `no such task <id>` when no task has that id. | | `list` | Writes every open task as `<id> <title>`, in the order the tasks were added. | ## What to add 1. `prio <id> <p>` sets a task's priority, where `p` is a digit from 0 to 9, and writes `prio <id> <p>`. A task nobody set a priority on has priority 5. An id no task has writes `no such task <id>`; a `p` outside 0 to 9 writes `bad priority <p>` and changes nothing. 2. `list` now orders the open tasks by priority, ascending, and breaks ties by id, ascending. Its line format does not change. 3. `list all` writes **every** task, finished ones included, under the same order, as `<mark> <id> <title>` — where the mark is `-` for an open task and `x` for a finished one. 4. A line whose first word is none of these commands writes `? <word>`, naming that first word. Today the program ignores such a line. Everything the program already does keeps working exactly as it does now. ## Done The job is finished when the program builds, the four additions behave as written, and the original three commands are unchanged. There are no tests in the directory; the contract above is the specification. ./Cargo.toml ./Cargo.lock ./BRIEF.md ./src/main.rs

content.text:
The tracker now does all four additions, and the three original commands behave as before. Clippy builds it with no warnings. There are no tests in the directory, so I checked it by running a sample command file. Every output matched the brief: priorities, `bad priority` and `no such task` messages, `list` and `list all` ordering with `-`/`x` marks, and `? frobnicate` for an unknown command. All changes are in `src/main.rs`: - **Priority:** each task now carries a priority, which starts at 5. - **`prio

`:** `p` must be a single digit from 0 to 9; anything else writes `bad priority

` and changes nothing. - **`list` and `list all`:** both sort by priority, then by id. Only the exact form `list all` shows finished tasks. Any other text after `list` (such as `list foo`) still lists just the open tasks, as before. - **Unknown commands:** a line whose first word isn't a command now writes `? `. The brief didn't cover a few cases, so I chose these: - **Both id and priority bad:** `prio` checks the id first, the same way `done` does. So `prio 99 x` writes `no such task 99`, not `bad priority x`. - **Non-numeric id in `prio`:** it writes `no such task `. A non-numeric id in `done` still crashes the program, as it always has; I left that alone. - **Lines of only spaces:** these are ignored like blank lines rather than reported as `? `. Before, they were silently ignored as well. - **Windows line endings:** if the command file uses them, a line like `list` ends in an invisible carriage return. It would now print `? list` instead of being silently ignored. I didn't strip those characters, because doing so would also change the titles that `add` records.
